Query Expansion

What if query is wrong?


Instead of sending the raw user query to the retriever, transform it first to improve retrieval performance.



more queries (multi-query, decomposition)
different query (HyDE, step-back)
different destination (routing)

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Multi-Query Retrieval
Generate multiple phrasings of the query, retrieve for each and apply Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF):


prompt = f"""Generate `{3-5}` different phrasings of the following question.
Each phrasing should approach the question from a different angle.

Original: {query}

Phrasings (one per line):"""

Sub-Question Decomposition

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
HyDE - Hypothetical Document Embeddings
Problem: Users write queries in natural language; documents use technical terminology. The embedding distributions don’t align well.
Solution: Generate a hypothetical document that would answer the query, then embed that document for retrieval:
prompt = f"""Write a short document passage that would directly answer
the following question. Write as if you're the source document.

Question: {query}

Passage:"""



Why it works: The hypothetical document has the vocabulary, tone, and structure of a real answer - better alignment with the indexed documents.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Step-Back Prompting (Zheng et al., 2023)
Abstract the specific question to a more general principle, retrieve on the abstraction:
Query: “why does vllm use paged attention”
Step-back Rewrite: “what are techniques for efficient memory management in LLM inference”

Useful for multi-hop reasoning where the direct query is too specific to match any single document.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Query Routing
Query: “Summarize the discussion so far”


No chunk in the vector store will match this query, since it’s a meta-question about the conversation, not about the indexed documents.



Solution : After query translation, send the query to the right data source.


Many RAG systems have multiple data sources:

Vector store for indexed documents
Web search API for current events
Relational database for structured data
Direct LLM fallback for general knowledge questions
refuse / ask a clarifying question

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Query Routing

Routing decides where the question goes.
Logical Routing: A classifier determines the question type and routes accordingly.
Semantic Routing: Use exemplar queries for each data store. Embed the question and compare it to query embeddings to determine the most relevant data source.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Dense Retrieval - Single Vector Bottleneck
Every bi-encoder

takes a document with m tokens and query with n tokens,
runs them through a transformer (producing m and n contextualized token vectors)
pools all vectors into a single d-dimensional vector.





A 200 token chunk enters the encoder as 200 x 768 = 153,600 numbers and leaves as 768.
99.5% of the representation is lost and a weighted average remains.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Single Vector Bottleneck
What is lost in pooling:

A movie review has information about actors, plot, cinematography, and score
A model trained on actor-focused queries will encode actor information preferentially
If you ask about the plot, the pooled vector has discarded that signal
Pooling forces conflicting signals into one representation — they interfere with each other



“Out-of-domain generalization” and “long context” are the two places where the bi-encoder’s pooling bottleneck hurts most.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Full interaction Retrieval Models



Contextually rich, effectively capture nuanced contextual relationships between the search query and the document.
Extremely computationally expensive because all documents have to be processed at query time




Great for second-stage retrieval (reranking), not first stage

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
section: Late Interaction Models [ColBERT, Khattab et al., 2020]
text:
Late Interaction Models [ColBERT, Khattab et al., 2020]
Late interaction

keep all token-level representations instead of pooling them
defer the query–document interaction until retrieval time.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Interaction Between Query and Document

Never (bi-encoder): both pooled, compared once at the end. Fast, lossy.
Immediately (cross-encoder): joint forward pass, attention everywhere. Accurate, unindexable.
Late (ColBERT): encode separately - so documents still precompute - but keep every token vector and let them interact at query time.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Evaluation Metrics - Retrieval
Unranked metrics
Do the right documents appear in the retrieved set?
Precision@k
\[
\text{Precision@k}=\frac{|\text{relevant docs in top-}k|}{k}
\]

Of the retrieved chunks, how many are relevant?
Low precision adds noisy context and can confuse the LM.


Fix

Improve embeddings/reranking so relevant chunks score higher.
Reduce k to improve precision (with possible recall drop).

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Evaluation Metrics - Retrieval
Unranked metrics
Recall@k
\[
\text{Recall@k}=\frac{|\text{relevant docs in top-}k|}{|\text{total relevant docs}|}
\]

Of all relevant chunks, how many were retrieved in top-k.
If recall is low, the answer evidence may never reach the LM.
Key intuition: No retrieval -> no grounded generation.


How to improve recall

Increase k (then control noise with reranking).
Use stronger retrievers / query expansion.
Improve chunking and document coverage in the index.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Evaluation Metrics - Retrieval
Ranked metrics : are the right documents ranked higher?
MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank): \[\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{|Q|} \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{\text{rank of first relevant doc}}\]

measures how high the first relevant document is ranked on average
sensitive to the position of the first relevant document, but ignores subsequent relevant documents

nDCG@k (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain): \[\text{nDCG@k} = \frac{\text{DCG@k}}{\text{IDCG@k}}, \quad \text{DCG@k} = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\text{rel}_i}{\log_2(i+1)}\]

Handles graded relevance (0/1/2 relevance levels)
nDCG@10 is the dominant retrieval metric (used in BEIR, MTEB)
Discount factor rewards ranking relevant docs higher

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Evaluation Metrics - Generation
Faithfulness: does the generated answer accurately reflect the retrieved information?
\[\text{Faithfulness} = \frac{\text{Number of answer claims supported by context}}{\text{Total number of claims in the answer}}\]


Example
Retrieved context: “The capital of France is Paris.”

Answer 1: “The capital of France is Paris. It is known for the Eiffel Tower.”
Answer 2: “The capital of France is Lyon. It is known for its cuisine.”


Scores

Answer 1: high faithfulness (1/2 claims supported)
Answer 2: low faithfulness (0/2 claims supported)

Low faithfulness => hallucination

Fix:

Improve prompting (do not guess, cite retrieved chunks)
Improve retrieval to provide more relevant context

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Evaluation Metrics - Generation
Answer Relevance: does the generated answer correctly answer the question?
\[\text{Answer Relevance} = \frac{\text{Number of answer sentences addressing the question}}{\text{Total number of sentences in the answer}}\]


Example
Question: “What is the capital of France?”

Answer 1: “The capital of France is Paris. It is known for the Eiffel Tower.”
Answer 2: “France is a country in Europe. It has many famous landmarks.”


Scores

Answer 1: high relevance (2/2 sentences address the question)
Answer 2: low relevance (0/2 sentences address the question)

Low relevance => model generates true but off-topic content

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
section: Constructing Ground Truth for RAG Evaluation
text:
Constructing Ground Truth for RAG Evaluation

Small datasets (50–100 questions):

Build Question–Answer–Chunk triples manually.
Manual curation avoids hallucinated supporting chunks and improves reliability.

Large datasets:

Use LLMs to draft ground-truth answers and chunks.
Have human annotators verify each generated triple.

Then evaluate:

Run RAG evaluation using frameworks like RAGAS.

text:
Retrieval Paradigm Selection








Situation
Recommended stack




Fewer than ~1,000 documents
Skip retrieval — put them in the context window


General English QA, ≲1M docs
Bi-encoder (E5/BGE) + BM25 + RRF → rerank


Exact IDs, codes, part numbers matter
BM25 is mandatory as the sparse half


High-stakes or out-of-domain (legal, medical)
ColBERT — every token carries evidence


Long chunks (> 512 tokens)
ColBERT, or chunk smaller


PDFs where the answer is in figures/tables
ColPali (or caption-then-retrieve)


Multilingual / cross-lingual corpus
mE5 or Qwen3-Embedding + bge-reranker-v2-m3


Latency < 50 ms on commodity hardware
Bi-encoder alone — skip the reranker





Production default: BM25 + bi-encoder + RRF, then cross-encoder rerank the top 50. Add anything fancier only where you can show it wins on your own eval set.

title: RAG - Advanced Retrieval Techniques and Evaluation
text:
Key Takeaways


Retrieval fails in two ways - you asked the wrong question, or the index can’t represent the answer. Every technique today is one or the other.
Pooling is lossy by design - a bi-encoder compresses n token vectors into one. Late interaction keeps them and defers the comparison to query time.
MaxSim is soft term matching - each query token finds its best match independently, so concepts stop interfering with each other.
Reranking is the cheapest big win - retrieve wide for recall, rerank narrow for precision.
Un-measured is un-improved - four metrics, and the pair you’re worst at tells you which half of the pipeline to fix.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
From Pixels to Tokens

A 3D tensor: [height, width, 3] of pixel intensities (RGB).
Goal: produce a sequence-of-vectors representation.




Each grid cell is now a token in a 196-word sentence describing this image and the transformer’s job is to process these tokens just like it would a sentence of English words.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Vision Transformer (ViT)

Dosovitskiy et al., ICLR 2021, arXiv:2010.11929






Split a 224×224 image into 16 pixel × 16 pixel patches -> 14×14 = 196 patches.
Flatten each patch (16·16·3 = 768 numbers).
Linearly project each flattened patch to dim \(d\) (e.g., 768).
Add a learned positional embedding (per-patch).
Run through a standard transformer encoder stack.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Code example: ViT
IMG_SIZE, PATCH, DIM = 224, 16, 768
x = to_tensor(img).unsqueeze(0)                 # [1, 3, 224, 224]
patchify = nn.Conv2d(3, DIM, kernel_size=PATCH, stride=PATCH)
tok = patchify(x).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)    # [1, 196, 768]  <- a "sentence"

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
CLIP

We have ~400M (image, caption) pairs scraped from the web.
We want an image encoder whose outputs are near the matching caption’s text-encoder output and far from non-matching captions.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
CLIP : Contrastive Pretraining
For a batch of \(N\) pairs, compute the \(N \times N\) similarity matrix \(S\), where \(S_{ij} = \cos(\text{img}_i, \text{txt}_j)\). The diagonal entries are positive pairs; off-diagonal are negatives.
InfoNCE loss: apply cross-entropy on rows (each image picks the right caption) and on columns (each caption picks the right image):
\[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ \log \frac{\exp(S_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(S_{ij}/\tau)} + \log \frac{\exp(S_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(S_{ji}/\tau)} \right]\]
where \(\tau\) is a learnable temperature

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
CLIP Applications

Zero-shot classification: to classify an image into ImageNet classes, encode each class name with the text encoder (‘a photo of a {class}’), encode the image, pick the highest cosine similarity. No labels needed.
Cross-modal retrieval: the workhorse that powers the RAG module’s multimodal retrieval.

Demo : CLIP zero-shot classification

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
SigLIP

CLIP’s softmax loss requires every example to know about every other example
SigLIP (Zhai et al., Google, ICCV 2023) replaces softmax with a per-pair sigmoid

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{SigLIP}} = -\sum_{i,j} \log \sigma\left(y_{ij} \cdot (t \cdot \mathbf{x}_i \cdot \mathbf{y}_j + b)\right)\]
where \(y_{ij} = +1\) for positives, \(-1\) for negatives, and \((t, b)\) are learnable.

Used in PaliGemma, Gemma 3, Qwen3-VL (SigLIP-2), and many others


What’s Next :

CLIP’s vision encoder is aligned with CLIP’s text encoder, not with Llama’s or Qwen’s text embeddings.
We can’t just hand CLIP vision vectors to Llama and expect it to read them.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text: From Understanding to Generation

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Fusion : Connecting Encoder to LLM
We have:

A frozen text LLM (eg Llama-3-8B) that consumes token-embedding sequences in dim \(d_\text{llm}\).
A frozen, language-aligned vision encoder (SigLIP) that produces patch-embedding sequences in dim \(d_\text{vis}\).


How to connect them?
Can we naively concatenate them:

Dimensions don’t match (\(d_\text{vis} \neq d_\text{llm}\)).
Semantic spaces don’t match (SigLIP’s “language space” \(\neq\) Llama’s input-embedding space).
The LLM was never trained to attend to non-text tokens.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Flamingo (DeepMind, 2022): gated cross-attention


Pros: LLM mostly frozen; supports interleaved images-and-text in long contexts (few-shot in-context multimodal prompting).
Cons: Heavy architectural modifications on the LLM, hard to extend to a new modality, lots of new parameters.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
BLIP-2 : Q-Former






A small transformer (“Querying Transformer”) with \(k\) learnable query tokens (typically 32).
The Q-Former cross-attends to the ViT output and produces 32 summary vectors regardless of input image size.
These 32 vectors are linearly projected to LLM dim and prepended to text tokens.
Trains ~188M params (the Q-Former). Vision encoder (~1B ViT-g) and LLM (3–11B) frozen.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text: Modern Vision-Language Models

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
LLaVA : the MLP projector


A 2-layer MLP with GELU maps each vision-encoder output vector (dim ≈ 1024) to LLM embed dim (e.g., 4096).
Projected vision tokens are concatenated with text-token embeddings to form a single sequence.
Hand the joint sequence to the LLM as if it were one long text prompt.

title: Large Multimodal Models
section: The LLaVA training recipe (Stage 1 : Feature Alignment)
text:
The LLaVA training recipe (Stage 1 : Feature Alignment)
Template used by most VLMs:

Freeze : vision encoder (CLIP-ViT) + LLM (Viccuna)
Train: only the MLP projector.
Data: 558K image-caption pairs filtered from LAION-CC-SBU.
Loss: standard next-token prediction on the caption, conditioned on the image.
Outcome: the projector learns to map SigLIP/CLIP-space into Llama-input-space. Caption-style outputs.

title: Large Multimodal Models
section: The LLaVA training recipe (Stage 2 : Instruction Tuning)
text:
The LLaVA training recipe (Stage 2 : Instruction Tuning)

Unfreeze: LLM (full or LoRA). Vision encoder stays frozen.
Train: projector + LLM.
Data: 150K GPT-4-generated multimodal instructions + ~515K academic VQA data.
Loss: same next-token prediction, but on instruction-style multi-turn conversations.
Outcome: the model can follow multimodal instructions, do reasoning, multi-turn dialog.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
A minimal VLM
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class MiniVLM(nn.Module):
    """A LLaVA-style multimodal LLM"""

    def __init__(self, vision_encoder, llm, vis_dim, llm_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.vision = vision_encoder            # SigLIP, frozen
        self.proj   = nn.Sequential(            # the MLP projector
            nn.Linear(vis_dim, llm_dim),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(llm_dim, llm_dim),
        )
        self.llm = llm                          # Llama-style decoder

    def forward(self, pixel_values, input_ids, image_token_id):
        # 1. Encode the image
        vis = self.vision(pixel_values).last_hidden_state  # [B, N_patches, vis_dim]
        vis = self.proj(vis)                                # [B, N_patches, llm_dim]

        # 2. Get text embeddings
        txt = self.llm.embed_tokens(input_ids)              # [B, N_text, llm_dim]

        # 3. Splice vis vectors in where the <image> placeholder sits
        x = splice_image_at_placeholder(txt, vis, input_ids, image_token_id)

        # 4. Standard LLM forward pass on the joint sequence
        return self.llm(inputs_embeds=x)

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Audio Representation

A 1D waveform: amplitude vs. time, typically sampled at 16 kHz for speech.
30 seconds of audio = 480,000 samples. Far too long to feed directly.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Preprocessing: log-mel spectrogram

Slide a 25 ms window over the waveform with a 10 ms stride.
For each window, compute the power spectrum, then apply 80 mel filterbanks (perceptually-spaced frequency bins).
Take the log.
Result: a 2D matrix of shape [80 mel bins, ~3000 time frames] per 30-second clip.



A spectrogram looks like an image: width is time, height is frequency, intensity is energy. The same encoder ideas that worked for ViT should work here

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Whisper Architecture


Input: log-mel spectrogram of shape [80, 3000] (30 seconds @ 16 kHz).
Stem: two Conv1d layers over the time axis (kernel=3, stride=2 on the second). This is the audio analog of ViT’s patchify. Halves the time dimension.
Output of stem: [1500, d] - a sequence of 1500 audio “patches” (each = 20 ms of audio).
Encoder: standard transformer with sinusoidal positional embeddings.
Decoder (Whisper-specific): transformer decoder that cross-attends to encoder output and produces text tokens (BPE, same as GPT-2). Predicts language ID + transcription + timestamps via special tokens.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Audio Generation
Task : How to autoregressively generate a waveform?

Solution : discrete audio codec tokens

A neural audio codec (e.g., EnCodec, SoundStream) compresses raw audio into a small sequence of discrete tokens (~50-75 tokens/second) using a learned VQ-VAE-style tokenizer.
A neural vocoder reverses the process: discrete tokens -> waveform.
Once audio is discrete, an autoregressive LLM can generate it just like text.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Qwen3-Omni : SotA in 2025-26

Inputs: text, image, video, audio -> each encoded by its respective tower, projected, and concatenated. Same fusion pattern as everything we’ve seen.
Audio encoder: Qwen3-Omni replaced Whisper with AuT (Audio Transformer) -> trained from scratch on 20 million hours of supervised audio
Two sub-models on the output side, both MoE:

Thinker (MoE): the main LLM. Autoregresses over text tokens.
Talker (MoE): smaller streaming model that produces discrete audio codec tokens in real time -> vocoder -> speech.


Talker conditions only on audio and visual multimodal features -> not on Thinker’s text representations. Allows post processing of text output (e.g., add prosody, emotion) before generating speech.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Multimodal Inference Engineering

Token explosion & prefill dominance

For text LLM chat: - Prompt is usually short (100s–1000s of tokens). Decode dominates wallclock. - TTFT (time-to-first-token) is small relative to total response time.
For multimodal: A 7B VLM

Input : single 2048×1536 image, 50-token query

Vision tokens: ~1500. Total prefill tokens: ~1550.
Input : 4K page (e.g., a document) + 50 token query
Vision tokens: 10,000+. Total prefill tokens: 10,050+
Prefill becomes the bottleneck.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Quantizing Multimodal LLMs
The rule: quantize where the parameters are, keep precision where the information enters.








Component
Precision
Why




Vision / audio tower
BF16 / FP16
~5% of the weights, 100% of the perception


Projector
BF16 / FP16
~20M params. Nothing to save


LLM body
FP8 / INT8 / INT4 / NVFP4
~95% of the weights





An error in the LLM body is one noisy step among many; the residual stream absorbs it.
An error in the vision tower is a corrupted perception that every later layer then reasons about faithfully.


Garbage in, confidently reasoned garbage out.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Quantizing MLLMs : in practice
llm-compressor skips the vision tower by pattern, not by hand:
from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.modifiers.quantization import GPTQModifier

recipe = GPTQModifier(
    targets="Linear",
    scheme="W4A16",
    ignore=[
        "re:.*lm_head",
        "re:.*vision_tower.*",           # the ViT  - leave it alone
        "re:.*multi_modal_projector.*",  # the projector - too small to matter
    ],
)
oneshot(model=model, recipe=recipe, dataset=calib_ds)


The trap: most calibration pipelines assume text-only inputs. Calibrate an MLLM on text and you have tuned the LLM body for a distribution it never sees at serving time. Your calibration set must contain (image, text) pairs.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Does it survive quantization?
FP8 / INT8 on the LLM body, vision tower untouched:









Accuracy retained
Throughput




FP8 / INT8
>99% across vision benchmarks
up to 3.5×


INT4 (W4A16)
small but real loss, worst on OCR / dense text
best memory saving





2026 formats: NVFP4 / MXFP4 on Blackwell-class hardware - 4-bit weights and activations with per-block scales.
Ready-made: unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4 runs a 27B multimodal model in ~20 GB.



Benchmark the task you actually ship. Aggregate VQA scores hide OCR regressions.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Serving MLLMs : what changes
A text LLM server has one compute stage. An MLLM server has two.




Vision encoder
LLM body




Runs
once per image
once per token


Bound by
compute (FLOPs)
memory bandwidth


Scales with
pixels
sequence length




Three consequences for your serving config:

Image embeddings are cacheable. The encoder is deterministic given the image - the same document page re-queried 20 times need only be encoded once.
Prefill can stall the server. A 10,000-token page monopolises a step unless prefill is chunked.
Memory profiling needs a worst case. vLLM must know the maximum images per request to reserve KV cache.

title: Large Multimodal Models
text:
Serving with vLLM
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": 4, "video": 1}' \
  --mm-processor-kwargs '{"min_pixels": 200704, "max_pixels": 1003520}' \
  --mm-encoder-tp-mode data \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens 4096


--limit-mm-per-prompt : bounds the worst case. Too high wastes KV cache; too low rejects requests.
--mm-processor-kwargs : the token-budget dial. max_pixels caps tokens per image before the encoder runs.
--mm-encoder-tp-mode data : tensor-parallel the LLM, data-parallel the encoder - it is too small for TP to pay for its all-reduce.
--enable-prefix-caching : reuses image embeddings across requests.



Serving a multimodal checkpoint as text-only? --language-model-only --skip-mm-profiling never loads the tower.

Serving with SGLang
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
  --tp 2 \
  --context-length 131072 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 4096 \
  --enable-metrics


RadixAttention is the differentiator: SGLang keeps a prefix tree of KV cache, so a shared system prompt and a repeated image are reused automatically across requests - no cache key to manage.
Strongest fit: many requests over the same document or image set.

text: Motivation

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
The Memory Wall Problem
LLM inference is memory-bound, not compute-bound:





Each token requires full forward pass
KV-cache helps avoid recomputation but still requires:

Reading all model parameters every step
Computing attention against growing KV-cache
Sampling one token… then repeating











Key Observation


Many tokens are “easy” to predict (e.g., common words, code boilerplate, repetitive patterns). Verification of K candidate tokens costs approximately the same as generating 1 token!

title: Speculative Decoding
Speculative Decoding
text:
LLM Speculative Decoding

Small/fast draft model guesses next K tokens
Large model verifies all K in parallel (one forward pass!)
Accept correct prefix, resample from divergence point
Lossless: Sample from the exact same distribution!

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
LLM Speculative Decoding








Critical Insight


Scoring K tokens in parallel ≈ same latency as generating 1 token because:

Memory bandwidth is the bottleneck
GPU compute is underutilized in single-token generation
Parallel verification exploits available FLOPs

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
The Universal Framework
Draft -> Verify -> Accept/Reject

Draft: Generate K candidate tokens cheaply via a draft mechanism

Methods differ in HOW they draft (separate model, heads, n-grams)

Verify: Run target model on all candidates in parallel

Get true probabilities for each position
Single forward pass for all K tokens

Accept/Reject: Use rejection sampling to maintain target distribution

Accept prefix of correct tokens
Resample at first rejection point using modified rejection sampling



\[\text{Speedup} = \frac{K \cdot \alpha}{1 + \frac{T_{\text{draft}}}{T_{\text{verify}}}}\]
Where \(\alpha\) is the acceptance rate and \(K\) is the draft length.

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
The Foundation (2022-2023)
Two concurrent Google papers established the field:
Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (Leviathan et al., 2022)
Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling (Chen et al., 2023)

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Algorithm: Auto-regressive Sampling (ArS)


One token per forward pass. This is what we want to speed up.

title: Speculative Decoding
text: Algorithm: Speculative Sampling (SpS)

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Modified Rejection Sampling
Guarantees lossless sampling from target distribution:


Case 1: Target prob >= Draft prob \[p_{\text{target}}(x) \geq p_{\text{draft}}(x)\]
Always accept (target “likes” this token at least as much)

Case 2: Target prob < Draft prob
\[p_{\text{target}}(x) < p_{\text{draft}}(x)\]
Reject with probability \(\frac{p_{\text{draft}}(x) - p_{\text{target}}(x)}{p_{\text{draft}}(x)}\)
If rejected, resample from the residual distribution.








Theorem (Chen et al., 2023)


Modified rejection sampling guarantees that the final output distribution is identical to sampling from the target model alone.

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Modified Rejection Sampling: Illustrated
Example: Draft model proposes token “the” at position \(t+1\)

Intuition


The residual distribution captures what the target model “wanted more of” than the draft. Tokens the draft overestimated (like “the”) get zero residual probability. Tokens the target preferred more (like “a”, “this”) get the leftover mass — ensuring the combined process exactly matches the target distribution.







Step 1: Draft sampled “the” (\(p_d = 0.50\), \(p_t = 0.30\))
\(p_t < p_d\) → accept with prob \(\frac{p_t}{p_d} = \frac{0.30}{0.50} = 0.60\)


Step 2: Coin flip says reject! → resample from residual


Step 3: Compute residual \(p'(x) = \text{norm}(\max(0,\; p_t - p_d))\)

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Draft Model Options (Chen et al.)

Smaller models, same family

Easy to obtain, similar distribution, Different serving topology needed

Distilled model

Optimized for speculation, Training cost is high

N-gram

Zero overhead, no training, Limited to simple patterns

Early-exit self-speculation (LayerSkip)

Draft = the target’s own first E layers; no second model, needs early-exit-aware training

Results








Setup: 4B parameter draft model optimized for 16 TPU topology (matching 70B Chinchilla)
Performance: 1.8ms/token vs 14.1ms/token for target (7.8x theoretical)
Real-world: ~2-3x speedup depending on domain

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Limitations

Draft Model Acquisition:

Need a separate, well-aligned draft model
Training cost can be significant
Distribution shift between draft and target

Serving Complexity

Two models to serve and maintain
Different optimal topologies for different model sizes
Memory overhead of second model

Single Candidate

γ is static, but difficulty varies by context

title: Speculative Decoding
text: Medusa: No Separate Draft Model!

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Medusa Architecture (Cai et al., 2024)


Idea: Add K small “Medusa heads” on top of target model’s last hidden states
Head k: Predicts token at position t+k+1
Parameters: ~0.5% additional parameters per head
Training: Freeze backbone, train heads with cross-entropy loss

title: Speculative Decoding
Speculative Decoding
text: Medusa: Tree Attention Verification

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Medusa Training : MEDUSA-1: Frozen Backbone



Cross-entropy loss between MEDUSA head predictions and ground truth tokens
For ground truth token \(y_{t+k+1}\) at position \(t + k + 1\):

Loss for k-th head: \(L_k = -\log p_t^{(k)}(y_{t+k+1})\)
\(p_t^{(k)}(y)\) = probability of token y predicted by k-th head
Add weight \(\lambda_k\) to balance loss across different heads

Total MEDUSA loss: \[L_{MEDUSA-1} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} -\lambda_k \log p_t^{(k)}(y_{t+k+1})\]

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Medusa Training : MEDUSA-2 : Joint Training


Objective: Maintain base model capability while training heads.

Combined Loss: Add the backbone model’s cross-entropy loss to the MEDUSA loss.
Backbone Loss: \[L_{\text{LLM}} = -\log p_t^{(0)}(y_{t+1})\]
Balance: Use weight \(\lambda_0\) to balance the base model and Medusa heads.

Total MEDUSA-2 Loss: \[L_{\text{MEDUSA-2}} = L_{\text{LLM}} + \lambda_0 L_{\text{MEDUSA-1}}\]

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Medusa: Results





Results

Speedup: ~2-3× on average
Arithmetic Intensity : 41× operational intensity gain

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Medusa: Limitations
Key Limitations

Position-Independent Prediction: Head 2 doesn’t know what Head 1 predicted
Limited Information: Only sees top-layer features
No dependencies: Can’t model dependencies between draft tokens
Speedup plateaus: ~3× even with more heads








The Core Problem


Medusa heads predict position i+k independently of positions i+1, i+2, …, i+k-1. Lower acceptance rates for later positions in the draft.

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE Series: Feature-Level Autoregression

feature = the last-layer hidden state, the d-dimensional vector just before the LM head

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE : Core Innovation
Key Insight: Autoregression at the feature level is simpler than at the token level.


Features contain richer information than just next-token logits
predict next feature vector \(f_{n+1}\) instead of token \(t_{n+1}\)


feature = the last-layer hidden state, the d-dimensional vector just before the LM head

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE : Feature Uncertainty




Are features enough to predict the next feature?
pure feature-to-feature regression is ill-posed

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE : Architecture


Draft predicts f_{n+1} from previous features f_<=n and the embedding of the just-sampled token t_{n+1} (shifted by one).
Use predicted feature to compute token probabilities for next token
Tree structure allows multiple candidates to be verified in parallel

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE-1: Training
Training Loss \[L = L_{\text{fea}} + 0.1 \times L_{\text{token}}\]

L_fea: Regression loss for feature prediction
L_token: Classification loss for token prediction

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE-1 : Verification

Multi-Round Speculative Sampling
For tree-structured drafts:

Try candidate 1 with original p
If rejected -> residual p₁ = norm(max(0, p - p̂₁))
Try candidate 2 against p₁ (not original p!)
Continue until acceptance or exhaustion

Maintains invariant: sampling from “remaining” probability mass.

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE-1: Results


Speedup: ~3×
Average acceptance length τ: 3-4 tokens
Lossless: Provably maintains target distribution

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE-2: Context-Aware Speculation (2024)
Problem: Static tree structure wastes resources on “easy” vs “hard” tokens.


Acceptance rate is context-dependent, not just position-dependent
“10+2” : next token uncertain (=, +, etc.)
“10+2=” : next token almost certain (“1”)


Solution: Dynamic tree construction using draft model confidence

High confidence -> expand tree deeper
Low confidence -> prune, keep tree shallow

title: Speculative Decoding
text: EAGLE-2: Tree Expand

title: Speculative Decoding
text: EAGLE-2: Tree Rerank + Mask

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE-2: Results







Important


Performance

20-40% faster than EAGLE-1
No additional training required (reuses the EAGLE-1 draft head unchanged)
completely lossless
Context-aware: Easy contexts (code boilerplate) get deeper trees
Hard contexts (creative writing) get shallower, wider trees

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
EAGLE-3: Training-Time Test (2025)
Problem: EAGLE-1/2’s feature-regression loss caps the draft model and acceptance stopped improving with more training data.

Drop the feature loss: train the draft on its own multi-step rollouts - training-time test - so training matches how the draft is actually used at inference
Multi-layer fusion: draft consumes low + mid + high layer features from the target, not just the top layer
Result: 3–6.5× speedup, and acceptance now scales with draft training data

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)
Speculation moved into pretraining: the model ships with its own draft module.


Sequential MTP modules (DeepSeek-V3): module \(k\) = one transformer block predicting token \(t+k+1\) autoregressively, the causal chain is kept, unlike Medusa’s independent heads
Input at each step: \(\text{concat}(\text{RMSNorm}(h_{\text{prev}}),\ \text{RMSNorm}(\text{emb of shifted token}))\) - the same feature + shifted-token trick as EAGLE
Shared embedding + output head with the main model -> tiny extra cost

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Native MTP in Production

Now standard equipment: DeepSeek V3/V4, Qwen3-Next / Qwen 3.6, Gemma 4, GLM-4.x, MiMo, Nemotron, MiniMax …
Zero extra model to serve; draft lives in the checkpoint
First-class serving support- vLLM: deepseek_mtp, qwen3_next_mtp, gemma4_mtp, …; SGLang & TensorRT-LLM: native MTP paths
DSpark (next) is DeepSeek upgrading its own MTP drafter post-hoc - same weights, better speculation

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
DFlash: Block-Diffusion (parallel) Drafting


Draft = tiny diffusion model: fills K <mask> slots in one bidirectional pass - no serial draft loop
Conditioned on fused target context features (multi-layer, EAGLE-3 style) via cross-use of the target’s KV
Reuses target embedding + LM head; only the few middle draft layers are trained

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
DFlash: Results


4.6–6.1× lossless on math/code benchmarks vs 1.8–2.2× for EAGLE-3
Chat (MT-Bench) gains least (2.75×) - low predictability, the recurring theme
NVIDIA: up to 15× for gpt-oss-120b on Blackwell at equal interactivity (TensorRT-LLM integration)
Ships in vLLM speculators [arXiv:2602.06036]

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
DSpark: Parallel + Sequential Drafting


(1) Target decodes a token as usual
(2) Parallel block drafts all K slots at once; a tiny sequential block then refines them left-to-right (kills late-block “suffix decay”); each token gets a confidence score \(C_k\)
Hardware-aware prefix scheduler: keep only the draft prefix worth verifying under current load (here E, F, G kept — H dropped)
(3) Target verifies the kept prefix — standard accept/reject, still exact

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
DSpark in DeepSeek V4


Conditional acceptance stays flat ≈0.85–0.9 across all draft positions - the sequential block fixes the late-position decay that plagues AR drafters
60–85% faster per-user on V4-Flash, 57–78% on V4-Pro
Accepted length +26–31% vs EAGLE-3, +16–18% vs DFlash
Shipping: SGLang --speculative-algorithm DSPARK; drafter training open-sourced as DeepSpec (MIT)

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Where the Field Is Heading

Drafting going non-autoregressive: block diffusion (DFlash), semi-AR blocks (DSpark), no serial draft loop
Verification becomes adaptive: confidence-scheduled, load-aware verify windows instead of a fixed K
Speculation moving into pretraining: native MTP heads are begin shipped along with models

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Model-Free Drafting
No draft model at all

N-gram / prompt-lookup: match the last few generated tokens against the prompt + output so far; propose whatever followed last time

vLLM ngram / ngram_gpu; HF prompt_lookup_num_tokens

Suffix Decoding (Snowflake Arctic): a suffix tree over previous outputs + current prompt; drafts long continuations, adaptively sized per step

2.3–6.3× on agentic pipelines; vLLM suffix method

Where they win: agents (tool-call loops), RAG, code editing, self-refinement - anywhere output repeats input

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Demo 1: Hugging Face Transformers






Setup


Using assistant_model parameter for automatic speculative decoding.



from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch
import time

# Target model (large)
model_name = "unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-bnb-4bit"
assistant_name = "double7/vicuna-68m"  # Tiny assistant

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name, 
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto"
)
assistant = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    assistant_name,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto"
)

prompt = "Explain quantum computing in simple terms:"
inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)

# Baseline
start = time.time()
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
baseline_time = time.time() - start
print(f"Baseline: {baseline_time:.2f}s")

# With speculative decoding
start = time.time()
outputs = model.generate(
    **inputs, 
    assistant_model=assistant,
    max_new_tokens=100
)
spec_time = time.time() - start
print(f"Speculative: {spec_time:.2f}s")
print(f"Speedup: {baseline_time/spec_time:.2f}x")

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
When to Use Speculative Decoding?


✅ Best For

Low batch sizes (1-16): Memory-bound regime
Interactive applications: Chatbots, coding assistants
Repetitive content: Code generation, structured outputs
Latency-sensitive: Real-time applications
Greedy decoding: Highest acceptance rates


❌ Avoid When

High batch + short context: Compute-bound, benefits diminish

2026 update: at long context the KV-cache is the bottleneck — speculation keeps paying even at batch 256 (MagicDec); modern schedulers adapt to load (DSpark) instead of switching off

Very high temperature: Acceptance rate drops
Creative writing: Unpredictable tokens, low acceptance
Memory constrained: Draft model adds overhead








Rule of Thumb


If your GPU utilization is <50% during decoding, speculative decoding will likely help. Check with nvidia-smi or profiling tools.

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Integration with Other Optimizations
Speculative decoding is orthogonal to other techniques:

Quantization: Can quantize both draft and target (e.g., FP8, INT8)
FlashAttention: Works seamlessly with tree attention
Continuous Batching: Needs careful KV cache management for rejected branches
Prefix Caching: Draft tokens can use cached prefixes
Disaggregated Serving: EAGLE-3 works with prefill-decode disaggregation







KV Cache Management


Naive approach: Discard all draft entries, recompute for accepted ones.
Better: Selective retention (EAGLE’s approach) - Keep KV for accepted path only - Discard KV for rejected branches - Track cache positions corresponding to tree nodes

Recap: Continuous Batching


Dynamically batch requests at the token level, allowing for early return and better GPU utilization.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Recap: Paged Attention


Logical blocks: The model’s attention mechanism operates on the entire context as a single logical block (e.g., a 16K token context treated as one block for attention computations).
Physical blocks (pages): Memory is divided into smaller physical blocks/pages (e.g., 16–32 tokens each), dynamically allocated and mapped to different requests as needed.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Paged KV Cache

Paged Attention 
Each request’s KV cache is divided into multiple physical blocks (pages) that can be allocated independently.
Multiple requests can share the same physical blocks if they have similar context lengths, improving memory efficiency and GPU utilization.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Paged Attention


PagedAttention allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space
During the attention computation, the PagedAttention kernel identifies and fetches different KV blocks separately
Computes attention across these non-contiguous blocks
This is done in a custom CUDA kernel optimized for the block-table lookup pattern

text:
Choosing Your Stack: Scenario-Based

Scenario 1:
“Run a chatbot on my desktop / laptop” -> llama.cpp with Q4_K_M quantization, Metal backend. Full privacy, no cloud needed.


Scenario 2:
“Serve Llama-70B to 100 concurrent users on 4× A100” -> vLLM or SGLang with tensor parallelism. Enable prefix caching for chat workloads.


Scenario 3:
“Structured JSON extraction from documents at scale” -> SGLang — RadixAttention maximizes prefix reuse for repeated templates, compressed FSM for structured output.


Scenario 4:
“Deploy DeepSeek-R1 across a 64-GPU cluster” -> NVIDIA Dynamo with disaggregated serving, vLLM or TRT-LLM backend. Smart router for KV cache locality.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Key Takeaways

Prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bound
Continuous batching (Orca) eliminates idle GPU time by scheduling at iteration level -> 2-36× throughput over static batching
PagedAttention (vLLM) eliminates KV cache fragmentation with OS-inspired virtual memory -> reduces waste from 60-80% to <4%, enabling 2-4× more throughput
Prefix caching avoids redundant prefill computation -> 5-20× TTFT reduction for workloads with shared prefixes
Disaggregated serving (DistServe) separates prefill and decode onto different GPUs -> independent optimization and 1.4-2.35× throughput improvement
Production orchestration (NVIDIA Dynamo) adds smart routing, dynamic scaling, KV cache management, and SLO-aware planning across GPU clusters -> up to 7× throughput on Blackwell

section: Recap: Model Size and Memory Requirements
text:
Recap: Model Size and Memory Requirements
For Inference :

Model size: number of parameters × bits per parameter
Memory requirements: model size + KV cache + activations

\[\text{Decode tokens/sec} \approx \frac{\text{Memory Bandwidth (GB/s)}}{\text{Model Size (GB)} + \text{KV Cache Overhead (GB)}}\]

Three numbers determine decode performance:

Memory bandwidth of GPU (more the better)

Model size in bytes (reduce with quantization)
KV cache size (reduce with GQA, MLA, sliding window)

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Key Inference Optimizations
Most optimizations map to one of four strategies:

Read less data per token

Quantization (smaller weights), GQA/MLA (smaller KV cache), pruning

Do more useful work per data read

Batching (amortize weight reads), kernel fusion (fewer HBM round trips)

Generate more tokens per forward pass

Speculative decoding (verify N tokens in one pass instead of generating 1)

Schedule / place work better


Continuous batching, prefix caching, prefill/decode disaggregation

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Representing Numbers

Data is stored as a sequence of bits (0 or 1)
Byte: 8 bits
Number storage depends on the number type:

Unsigned integer: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Integer: 0, −1, 1, −2, 2, −3, 3, …
Real values: 12.34, −0.001, …

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Unsigned Integer

Each bit represents a power of 2
Number = sum of powers corresponding to positions with a 1

Example:

= 1×2⁶ + 1×2⁴ + 1×2² + 1×2¹ = 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 86



Type
Range




UINT8 (8-bit unsigned)
0 to 255


UINT16 (16-bit unsigned)
0 to 65,535


UINT32 (32-bit unsigned)
0 to 4,294,967,295

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Signed Integer

Each bit represents a power of 2, with the most significant bit (MSB) representing the sign
Number = sum of powers corresponding to positions with a 1, considering the sign bit


Example: Writing -86 in 8-bit signed integer format: 1. Start with the positive value 86: 01010110 2. Invert the bits: 10101001 3. Add 1: 10101010
= -1 x 2⁷ + 1×2⁶ + 1×2⁴ + 1×2² + 1×2¹ = -128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = -86



Type
Range




INT8 (8-bit signed)
-128 to 127


INT16 (16-bit signed)
-32,768 to 32,767


INT32 (32-bit signed)
-2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Real Values (Floating Point)

Represented using a sign bit, exponent bits, and mantissa (fraction) bits
Number = (-1)^(sign) × (1 + mantissa) × 2^(exponent - bias)


sign - 1 bit - positive or negative
exponent - 8 or 5 bits - determines the range of representable numbers
mantissa - 23 or 10 bits - determines the precision of representable numbers

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Quantization for LLMs

Pick expensive layers and quantize them to 4 or 8 bits, while keeping the rest in 16 or 32 bits
Quantization can be applied to:

Weights: the parameters of the model
Activations: the intermediate outputs of the model during inference




Feed-forward and attention projection layers account for ~95% of parameters and 65–85% of computation
Goal:

Quantize these parameters to fewer bits (e.g., BF16/FP16 → INT8)
Use low-bit-precision matrix multiplication

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
8-Bit Quantization: Absmax (Symmetric Quantization)
How : Scale the FP32 values to fit within the INT8 range of [-128, 127] by dividing by the maximum absolute value in the matrix and multiplying by 127.




Formula:
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}} &= \text{round}\!\left(\frac{127}{\max|\mathbf{X}|} \cdot \mathbf{X}\right) \\[6pt]
\mathbf{X}_{\text{dequant}} &= \frac{\max|\mathbf{X}|}{127} \cdot \mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}}
\end{aligned}\]


x = np.array([-3.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0])

# calculate the scale factor
if np.max(np.abs(x)) != 0:
    scale = 127.0 / np.max(np.abs(x))
else:
    scale = 1.0

# apply scaling
x_quantized = np.round(x * scale).astype(np.int8)
x_dequantized = x_quantized.astype(np.float32) / scale

title: Quantization for LLMs
text: 8-bit Quantization: Zero-point (Asymmetric Quantization)

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
8-bit Quantization: Zero-point (Asymmetric Quantization)
How : Scale the FP32 values to fit within the INT8 range of [-128, 127] by dividing by the range of the values and adding a zero-point to shift the values into the INT8 range.


Formula:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{scale} &= \frac{255}{\max(\mathbf{X}) - \min(\mathbf{X})} \\
\text{zeropoint} &= -\text{round}(\text{scale} \cdot \min(\mathbf{X})) - 128
\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}} &= \text{round}\!\left(\text{scale} \cdot \mathbf{X} + \text{zeropoint}\right) \\
\mathbf{X}_{\text{dequant}} &= \frac{\mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}} - \text{zeropoint}}{\text{scale}}
\end{aligned}\]

def zeropoint_quantize(x):
    x_min = torch.min(x)
    x_max = torch.max(x)

    qmin, qmax = -128, 127

    if x_max - x_min != 0:
        scale = (qmax - qmin) / (x_max - x_min)
    else:
        scale = 1.0
        
    zero_point = torch.round(qmin - x_min * scale)
    zero_point = torch.clip(zero_point, qmin, qmax).to(torch.int8)
    x_quantized = torch.round(x * scale + zero_point)
    x_quantized = torch.clip(x_quantized, qmin, qmax).to(torch.int8)
    x_dequantized = (x_quantized.to(torch.float32) - zero_point) / scale
    return x_quantized, x_dequantized

LLM.int8()
Dettmers et al 2022

LLMs have outliers in their weight distributions, which can lead to large quantization errors when using simple techniques like absmax quantization.

Observation
Transformer LMs have outlier features — columns of activations that are unusually large.


In models with ≥ 6.7B parameters, an outlier occurs in 100% of layers
Hypothesis: quantization performance degrades significantly due to these outliers

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
LLM.int8()
Approach:
Perform computations involving outliers in higher precision (FP16), all other computations in lower precision (INT8), then merge the results.

Only ~0.1% of activation features are outliers

llama.cpp
Legacy quants come in two main subcategories that correspond to symmetric and asymmetric quantization:

Type 0 (symmetric): Q4_0, Q5_0, Q8_0
Type 1 (asymmetric): Q4_1, Q5_1, Q8_1

The Q in the naming convention indicates the bit width

for example, Q4 means (most) weights are stored as 4-bit integers
The _0 and _1 suffixes indicate the type.

Example : bartowski/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GGUF Q8_0

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
llama.cpp
K-quants : Uses scaling for block also, two level quantization for quatinzation of weights as well as blocks.

K-quants group 8 regular blocks into one super-block, creating a two-level hierarchy:

Regular blocks: Still contain 32 quantized weights each (e.g., INT4)
Block constants: Scale and offset for each regular block, now stored as INT8 (quantized!)
Super-block constants: One pair of FP16 constants to dequantize the block constants
The size modifiers (S/M/L) indicate the agressiveness of quantization

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
llama.cpp
I-quants: Vector quantization
Scalar quantization

Traditional quants (legacy and K-quants) quantize individual weights
w_i → integer_quant

Vector quantization
I-quants treat groups of 8 weights as indivisible
w_vec = [w_1, w_2, ..., w_8] → integer_quant

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
llama.cpp
Vector quantization is facillitated by a codebook of reference (or prototype) vectors, with entries of this form:
r_vec = [r_1, r_2, ..., r_8] → integer_code
group of weights - treated as a vector -> map to nearest vector in a codebook

More details at HF and gguf-docs

Quantization-aware training
Motivation: Fine-tune a model so that it is “prepared” for quantization at inference time.
Basic idea: Insert artificial quantize-dequantize operations into the computational graph during training.
# QAT: x_fq is still in float
# Fake quantize simulates the numerics of quantize + dequantize
x_fq = (x_float / scale + zp).round().clamp(qmin, qmax)
x_fq = (x_fq - zp) * scale
This allows the model to learn weights that are robust to quantization noise.
Example: Kimi-K2-Thinking uses QAT with native INT4 quantization in the post-training stage to achieve lossless 2× speed-up in low-latency mode.

text:
Prompting
Prompting is the process of designing input text to elicit desired outputs from a language model.

\(p_\theta(y|f(x))\) is the probability of output \(y\) given input \(x\) under model parameters \(\theta\).
x : “I love LLMs”
f(x) : “Translate to French: I love LLMs”
y : “J’aime les LLMs”

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Prompt Components
Most prompts consist of the following components:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Prompting Strategy : No Prompt
After pre-training, we have an autoregressive language model \(p(x_1, x_2, ..., x_T)\)
Prompt: \(x_{1:t}\) -> “When a dog sees a squirrel, it will usually”
Output: \(x_{t+1:T}\) ->

“bark a lot, especially at close range.”
“start to chase after it. When it does…”

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Prompting Strategy : Zero Shot Prompting

Zero-Shot Prompting

when you provide a task description and input without any examples

Prompt

f(x:instruction) = “Translate to French: I love LLMs”

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Few Shot Prompting

Few-Shot Prompting

when you provide a task description, input, and a few examples of input-output pairs.
provide (x,y) examples in the prompt
Prompt: \(f(x_{test}; instruction, [(x, y)_1, \ldots, (x, y)_K])\)
Output: y_test

Example:

prompt = f"""Translate the following English sentences to French.
English: I love LLMs
French: J'aime les LLMs
English: The weather is nice today
French:"""


Few-shot prompting is a powerful technique that allows the model to learn from examples without any parameter updates, often referred to as “in-context learning”.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
In-context Learning
In-context Learning

the ability of a language model to learn and perform tasks based on the context provided in the input prompt, without any parameter updates.



ICL: provide (input, output) pairs as examples

prompt = f"""Translate the following English sentences to French.
English: I love LLMs
French: J'aime les LLMs
English: The weather is nice today
French:"""



Ability to leverage many examples varies by model size and architecture

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Chain of Thought Prompting
Wei et al. (2022)

Encourage the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before giving the final answer.
Approach: Provide examples in the prompt that include the reasoning process, or explicitly ask the model to “think step by step”.
CoT with examples (few shot CoT)

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Chain of Thought Prompting

Models can generate reasoning steps even without examples



Chain of thought data in pretraining corpus may contribute to this ability, but explicit prompting can enhance it significantly.
System prompts that encourage step-by-step reasoning can also improve performance on complex tasks, even without few-shot examples.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text: CoT Benefits

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT Benefits
CoT prompting can significantly improve performance on complex reasoning tasks, especially as model size increases.

Interpretability: the LLM’s generated chain of thought can be used to better understand the model’s final answer.
Applicability: CoT prompting can be used for any task that can be solved by humans via language.
Prompting: no training or fine-tuning is required of any LLMs. We can just insert a few CoT examples into the prompt!

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT - Zeroshot

Even without examples, simply asking the model to “Let’s think step by step” can improve performance on reasoning tasks:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT - Self-Consistency

Instead of generating a single chain of thought, generate multiple reasoning paths and take a majority vote on the final answer:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT - Least-to-Most Prompting

Decompose a complex problem into a sequence of simpler subproblems, and solve them in order:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Limitations of Linear CoT

CoT follows left to right reasoning, but some problems may require exploring multiple reasoning paths in parallel, backtracking, lookahead or revisiting previous steps


No backtracking: Once a step is generated, the model cannot revise it
Local error propagation: Early arithmetic errors cascade irreversibly
Exploration vs. Exploitation: Single path cannot explore alternative solution strategies

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Tree of Thoughts (ToT) Prompting

Similar to Least to Most, but with more flexibility in how the subproblems are defined and solved

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Tree of Thoughts (ToT) Prompting

ToT allows for this by maintaining a tree of possible reasoning paths and exploring them systematically

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
ToT Example
MODEL = "gpt-5.3"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are an expert problem solver using Tree-of-Thought reasoning."""

USER_PROMPT = """
Using numbers 3, 7, 9, 25, reach 24 using +, -, *, /.

At each step:
1. Propose 3 candidate next operations
2. Evaluate each (score 1-10)
3. Pick the best and continue

Be structured and concise.
"""

def generate_thought(state):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": state}
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content


def tree_of_thought(max_steps=5):
    state = USER_PROMPT

    for step in range(max_steps):
        print(f"\n--- Step {step+1} ---")
        output = generate_thought(state)
        print(output)

        # Append reasoning to state (this is the "tree expansion")
        state += "\n" + output

    return state


if __name__ == "__main__":
    final_trace = tree_of_thought()

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
The System 1 / System 2 in LLMs
Modern LLMs exhibit two distinct operational modes that mirror Kahneman’s cognitive frameworks:


System 1 : Intuitive Pattern Matching

Immediate next-token prediction
Style transfer, translation, pattern completion
“The capital of France is ___” -> "Paris"


System 2 : Deliberate Reasoning

Multi-step computation requiring working memory
Mathematical derivation, logical deduction, multi-hop retrieval
“If a train travels 60 km/h for 45 min then 80 km/h for 90 min, what is the average speed?”

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
section: Why Does Externalizing Thought Help? (Computation-Depth View)
text:
Why Does Externalizing Thought Help? (Computation-Depth View)
A standard transformer has a fixed computation graph per token: \(L\) layers × \(H\) heads.

Each forward pass has bounded computation depth
Problems requiring more than \(O(L)\) serial steps cannot be solved in one pass
This holds regardless of model size


CoT : Emitting intermediate tokens lets the model recurse through its own weights

Turns a feed-forward network into something closer to a bounded-depth RNN
Each new token’s forward pass can read all prior intermediate tokens via attention



Theoretical results:

Feng et al. (2023): Constant-depth transformers provably cannot solve arithmetic or dynamic programming in one pass, but can with CoT of length linear in the input.




Takeaway: CoT converts a fixed-depth parallel computer into an adaptive-depth one — the theoretical justification for why reasoning-heavy tasks demand long output sequences.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
section: Why does CoT work at all?
text:
Why does CoT work at all?
1. Distributional shift

The trigger phrase shifts the output distribution toward text resembling worked examples from pre-training (textbooks, Stack Exchange, tutoring dialogues)


2. Scratchpad as adaptive compute

Each emitted token grants the model another forward pass conditioned on all prior tokens
The prompt effectively unlocks the computation-depth argument



These are not mutually exclusive : CoT works because

the model has seen such traces during pre-training and
emitting them unlocks additional serial compute.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text: CoT Limitations

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
The Faithfulness Problem
Unfaithful Reasoning: CoT may be post-hoc rather than true computation trace.

Intervention studies:

Suppression: Add “…therefore [wrong answer]” to CoT -> Model often follows conclusion despite contradictory reasoning
Augmentation: Add factual context mid-generation -> Model ignores new information if already committed to path



Self-Correction Paradox

Without external feedback, asking “Are you sure?” often degrades performance 
Effective self-correction requires either:

External verification (code execution, search)
Explicit training on self-refinement (RL with process rewards)

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Base vs Instruction-tuned Models

Base (Pre-trained) Models: Trained on massive datasets for next-token prediction.

Good at: Text completion, few-shot learning.
Example: smollm3-3B-base (Requires specific phrasing to evoke desired behavior).

Instruction-tuned (IT) Models: Fine-tuned on (Instruction, Output) pairs and preference data (RLHF/DPO).

Good at: Following direct commands, conversational dialogue, helpfulness, and safety.
Example: smollm3-3B (Optimized for chat interfaces).

Key Difference: Same architecture and (mostly) the same pre-trained knowledge, but the weights have been further tuned on instruction/preference data. IT models are conditioned to act as assistants and usually adhere to specific Chat Templates.

Why Reference-Based Evaluation Fails for LLMs?

Paraphrase insensitivity.

“The cat sat on the mat” and “On the mat sat the cat” - identical meaning , near-zero BLEU overlap.

No semantic grounding.

“Paris is the capital of France” (correct) and “Paris is the capital of Germany” (wrong), n-gram overlap can’t distinguish

Openness of the output space.

“write a haiku about autumn,” infinite valid outputs exist. No single reference or even 10 references covers the space.




SupportBot · Reference: “Returns are accepted within 60 days of delivery.” Reply: “You’ve got 60 days from when it arrived to send it back.” Exact match: 0. BLEU: near zero. The answer is perfect.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
When Reference-Based Evaluation Works

The output space is small and enumerable.

Classification, extraction, multiple choice.

The output is a structured object.

JSON schema validation, email IDs, format compliance etc.

A programmatic check is ground truth.

Code execution (does the test pass?), math (does sympy agree?), SQL (does the query return the same rows?).

Many others

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Three Gulfs Model


Gulf of Specification (Developer ↔︎ LLM Pipeline)

challenge of communicating your intent to the LLM

Gulf of Comprehension (Developer ↔︎ Data)

cannot manually review every input and output
there will be errors and outliers that are hard to spot at scale.

Gulf of Generalisation (Data ↔︎ LLM Pipeline)

LLM behaviour varies across inputs; it worked on your 5 examples
may need task decomposition, better retrieval, fine-tuning

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Three Gulfs Model

How to develop effective evaluation strategies that bridge these gulfs and enable us to build better LLM applications?


SupportBot ·

Specification: you never told it to ask for an RMA number on returns.
Comprehension: 50k conversations a week - we can read maybe few hundreds.
Generalisation: it handles “where is my order?” and fails “where are my orders?”




Reference-based metrics fail because of the gulfs - specifically Generalisation. So instead of better METRICs, we need a better PROCESS

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Eval Regimes
Evaluation breaks cleanly into three regimes.

Offline (pre-ship): Error analysis, synthetic data generation, LLM-as-judge development
Online (production): Monitoring with automated evaluators, guardrails, incident response
Guardrails (runtime): Real-time constraints and safety checks





SupportBot ·

Offline: does the new prompt still quote the 60-day window on 200 golden cases?
Online: did escalations to human agents go down this week?
Guardrail: block any reply containing a full card number - before it renders.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Offline Evaluation
Systematic testing against a fixed dataset before the changes / application reaches users.
What it answers.

Did this prompt change regress anything?
Is model A better than model B for this task?
What’s the baseline?


Implementation Strategies

Benchmark datasets (MMLU, HumanEval, HLE) - capability assessment.
Golden sets - curated, domain-specific, with reference answers or rubrics.
LLM-as-judge scoring.
Human annotation


Slow to run but run frequently during development (CI?)

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Online Evaluation
Measurement in production, on real users.
What it answers.

Are the users actually happier?
Did the business metric move?
Does offline testing correlate with real-world performance?


Implementation Strategies

A/B tests - show variant A to half, variant B to the other.
Implicit signals - session length, session abandonment, retry rate.
Explicit feedback - upvotes and downvotes, support tickets.
Shadow traffic - run the new model silently alongside the old, compare.


Slow to collect (days to weeks), noisy, but real signal that matters most.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Guardrails
Runtime checks on every single request/response, blocking on violations.
What it answers.

Is this output safe to return to the user right now?
PII leaks, prompt injection, off-topic responses, hallucinated citations.


Implementation Strategies

Input classifiers (toxic / jailbreak detection).
Output validators (JSON schema, regex, allowlist).
Safety LLMs-as-judges (fast, small).
Hard stops - refuse-to-answer, fallback templates.


Has to be fast, run synchronously in the critical path on every request, add to latency

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Example : NCERT Doubt Solver









Evaluation
When
Signal
Decision




Offline
Pre-ship
Expert judgments on golden set
Fix prompt, build evaluators


Online
Production
User satisfaction, engagement metrics
Roll out changes, monitor impact


Guardrails
Runtime
Safety violations, format errors
Block response, trigger fallback

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Task Decomposition
Component Level vs End-to-End Evaluation

End-to-end eval

Input goes in, final output comes out, you grade the output.
Pro : Measures what the user experiences. The only thing that ultimately matters.
Con : When it fails, you don’t know why. A bad answer could be bad retrieval, bad reranking, bad generation, or all three compounding.



Component-level eval
Each subsystem evaluated against its own inputs and outputs.

Pro : When a component regresses, you know where to fix.
Con : Components that each score 95% still compound: 0.95⁴ = 0.81. Four “excellent” stages give a system that fails one request in five. Component-level evals can also miss emergent failures that only appear end-to-end.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Task Decomposition - Example








Stage
Component eval
Metric




Retrieval
“Is the relevant doc in the top-k?”
Recall@k, MRR


Reranking
“Is the best doc on top?”
nDCG, precision@1


Generation
“Does the answer stay grounded in retrieved context?”
Faithfulness (LLM judge)


End-to-end
“Is the final answer correct?”
Exact-match / LLM judge

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
RAG Metrics

Recall@k: Do all relevant chunks for a query appear in your top K results? (most important)
Precision@k: Are the top-k retrieved documents relevant?
MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank): How high is the best relevant document ranked?
nDCG (normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain): Are relevant documents ranked higher than irrelevant?

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
What is a Trace?

To evaluate a component, we first have to be able to see it. That is what a trace gives.


“A trace is the complete record of all actions, messages, tool calls, and data retrievals from a single initial user query through to the final response. It includes every step across all agents, tools, and system components in a session.”


A complete trace includes:

The original user query
All retrieved documents/contexts
Every LLM call (prompt + response)
All tool calls and their results
The final output shown to the user
Metadata: latency, token usage, model version, prompt version




SupportBot · One trace = the user’s message, the classified intent, the policy chunks retrieved, the order_lookup call and its arguments, the generation prompt, the reply. Without the retrieved chunks you cannot tell “wrong policy found” from “right policy ignored.”

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Why traces matter?

Without full traces, you can’t distinguish retrieval failures from generation failures
Without tool call logs, you can’t tell if the agent chose the wrong tool or used it incorrectly
Without latency data, you can’t identify cost/performance regressions

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
The Evaluation Lifecycle
You can now see your system (traces) and you know what to measure (components, end-to-end).
The remaining question: what should you measure first?

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Why Error Analysis

LLMs have infinite surface area for potential failures. We cannot anticipate what will break.
Only after observing real failures can we define criteria that matter.
The act of reviewing data builds intuition that no automated system can replicate.
Automated evaluators built for imagined failure modes waste effort and miss real problems.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text: Five Stages of Error Analysis

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Stage 1 : Bootstrap an Initial Dataset
Have production traffic? Sample it.
Don’t yet? Generate synthetic queries.

Look into what are different dimensions / aspects of user queries?

SupportBot:

Feature: order tracking, returns, billing, contact search
Scenario: multiple matches, no matches, ambiguous request, invalid data, system error
Persona: new user, expert user, frustrated customer, non-native speaker


These three dimensions - feature × scenario × persona - come back in Step 2 when we build the judge’s dataset

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Stage 1 : Another Example
Example for a recipe app:

Dietary Restriction: vegan, gluten-free, none
Cuisine Type: Italian, Asian, comfort food
Query Complexity: simple request, multi-step, edge case

Tuple → natural language:

Generate structured tuples: (Vegan, Italian, Multi-step)
Convert to natural language: “I need a dairy-free lasagna recipe that I can prep the day before”

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Stage 1 : Dimensions in Practice
The same three axes, as tables you can hand to an expert:

Features → what the system does · Scenarios → what situation the user is in · Personas → who is asking

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Generating Synthetic Queries / Data
Two-step generation process:

Generate structured tuples: (Returns, Invalid Data Provided, Frustrated Customer)
Convert tuples to natural language: “i already sent you order 1234567890 twice, where is my refund”

Key rules:

Write 20 tuples by hand first (builds intuition about the problem space)
Start with failure hypotheses (what do you suspect will break?)
Run synthetic queries through your actual system to capture full traces
Sample 100 traces for error analysis


Fix obvious problems first - don’t generate synthetic data for issues you can fix immediately

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Generating Synthetic Queries / Data
When synthetic data may not be reliable:

Domains requiring deep expertise (medical, legal) where LLMs lack nuanced understanding
Scenarios where your system’s behavior changes the query distribution
Cases where the synthetic data doesn’t match real user intent patterns

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Stage 2 : Read and Label
Open Coding

Read raw traces, analyze them manually (Don’t delegate to an automated system like LLM)
Write free-form notes about what’s wrong

“quoted 30-day returns, policy is 60 - looks like an old doc”
“asked for account number before verifying who they are”
“user said address, bot changed the delivery date”
“three matching orders, bot picked one at random”
“tone is condescending”

Focus on observable problems, not hypothesized causes
Have a domain expert verbalize their thought process while reviewing. One hour of this surfaces more insight than days of automated analysis.


do this for 30-50 traces, more the better. Stop when you see the same problems repeated.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Stage 3 : Cluster Failure Modes
Axial Coding

Group similar problems into categories (failure modes)
SupportBot, from the notes on the previous slide:

stale_policy - answered from an outdated document
auth_bypass - requested sensitive data before verifying identity
intent_mismatch - solved a different problem than the one asked
ambiguity_unresolved - multiple candidates, picked one silently
tone - condescending or dismissive

Refine categories iteratively as you review more traces


Note what happened: five free-form notes became five named, countable failure modes. That naming is the whole of Stage 3.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
section: Stage 4 : Label Traces with New Taxonomy
text:
Stage 4 : Label Traces with New Taxonomy
Labeling

Go back through each trace and label it with your failure mode taxonomy
When you finish, start again from trace 1 and relabel everything
Why repeat the pass?

your understanding of the criteria has changed
your standards become more nuanced as you review more traces
you will notice issues you missed on the first pass

This shift in judgment is called evaluation criteria drift
Second-pass labeling produces more consistent and higher-quality annotations

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Stage 5 : Quantify and Iterate

Keep doing this till no new failure modes are seen
By the end, you should have a set of well-defined failure modes, each with examples from real traces

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Prioritization

Count how often each failure mode occurs
Estimate user impact for each (frustration, task failure, harm)
Prioritize: fix high-frequency + high-impact first
Add representative examples of each failure mode to your golden dataset

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Surfacing Problematic Traces
Initially, don’t wait for user complaints or rely on automated metrics.
Random Sampling (the baseline)

Review a random sample of traces
If you find few issues, escalate to stress testing: deliberately create queries that test your prompt constraints

Use Evals for Initial Screening

Use existing test suite if any. (Unit tests also work)
Do error analysis on flagged traces

Efficient Sampling

Outlier detection: unusually long conversations, sessions with multiple retries
Metric-based sorting: surface traces with anomalous scores
Stratified sampling: ensure coverage across user segments, query types, time periods

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Error Analysis - How Often?








System State
Review Frequency
Focus




New system
Weekly
Stabilize failure patterns; build initial taxonomy


Stable system, no changes
Monthly
Monitor for drift; sample 100+ fresh traces


After significant changes
Immediate
New features, prompt updates, model switches


Between major analyses
Weekly
10–20 traces, focusing on outliers


After incidents
Immediate
User complaint spikes, production alerts

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
From Error Analysis to Evaluations
You now have a ranked list of real failure modes, each with examples from real traces.

Next Question is: for each failure mode, what is the simplest thing that reliably catches it?

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
“Why Not Just Fix the Errors?”
You should. Fix easy ones first - most failure modes disappear after a few prompt edits. But some persist.









SupportBot mode
Cheapest fix
Outcome




stale_policy
delete the superseded doc from the index
gone


ambiguity_unresolved
prompt: “if more than one order matches, ask which”
mostly gone


intent_mismatch
prompt: “if the request is ambiguous, ask”
reduced - persists





But a fix cannot do two things:

Prove fixes. “I tried five examples and it looks better” is the vibe check.
Stay fixed. “Fixing 2 issues might introduce or regress 4 new ones.” Next prompt edit, next model version, next retrieval change.




Error analysis finds bugs. An evaluator keeps them fixed.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Cost-Benefit Hierarchy of Evaluation Methods










Evaluator Type
Build Cost
Maintenance Cost
When to Use




Assertions / regex checks
Minutes
Near zero
Objective constraints: JSON schema, required fields, format validation


Code-based checks
Hours
Low
Structured validation: fact extraction, numerical comparison, code execution


Reference-based comparison
Hours
Low
When you have known correct answers


LLM-as-Judge (general)
Days + 100+ labels
Weekly
Subjective qualities after exhausting cheaper options


LLM-as-Judge (specialized)
Days + 50+ labels per mode
Weekly
Specific failure modes that persist after prompt fixes




Core principle: Start with the cheapest method that could catch the failure, and escalate only when it doesn’t.

title: LLM Evaluation - II
text:
Cost-Benefit Hierarchy of Evaluation Methods








SupportBot failure mode
Cheapest check that catches it




auth_bypass
regex - reply asks for account number with no prior verification step


stale_policy
code check - does the cited policy ID match the current one?


ambiguity_unresolved
code check - >1 order matched but reply contains no clarifying question


intent_mismatch

tone
