text:
Continuous Batching
Continuous Batching:

Dynamically batch requests at the token level, allowing for early return and better GPU utilization.
As soon as one request in the batch finishes generating its next token, it can be returned to the client, while the remaining requests continue processing.


Early finished and late arrived requests are handled much more efficiently. The server can immediately return results for completed requests without waiting for the entire batch to finish, significantly reducing tail latency and improving user experience.

title: Inference Servers - I
text:
Continuous Batching Mechanics
The Loop:

Selection: Choose candidate requests for next iteration
Batch Formation: Combine prefill chunks and decode tokens
Forward Pass: Run model on current batch
Completion Check: Identify finished sequences
Admission: Add new requests from queue
Iteration: Repeat

Benefits:

No Waiting: Short requests exit immediately, don’t wait for long ones
GPU Saturation: Keep compute units busy 80%+ of time

Excample code : MinivLLM’s continuous batching loop

title: Inference Servers - I
text:
Chunked Prefill
A large prefill can dominate an iteration and spike latency for decode requests.
Chunked prefill addresses this:

Split large prefills into chunks (e.g., 512 tokens at a time)
Interleave prefill chunks with decode steps
Prevents a single large prefill from blocking decode for all other requests

This is now standard in vLLM (enabled by default) and SGLang.

title: Inference Servers - I
text:
Scheduling Policies


Scheduling

First-Come-First-Served (FCFS)
Priority-Based
Longest Prefix Match (LPM)





Preemption Strategies:

Swap: Move KV cache to CPU memory when preempting
Recompute: Discard KV cache, regenerate when resuming

Cost: 2× compute for the prompt
Benefit: No memory bandwidth cost for swap


Rule of Thumb: Swap for long sequences (KV cache >> compute cost), recompute for short sequences.

Generation Phase (Autoregressive Decoding):

title: Inference Servers - I
text:
KV Cache


Problem: Without caching, we recompute K and V for all previous tokens at every step!

Step 1: Compute K, V for token 1
Step 2: Recompute K, V for tokens 1, 2
Step 3: Recompute K, V for tokens 1, 2, 3
…
Step N: Recompute K, V for all N tokens → O(N²) redundant computation


Solution: KV Cache — Store computed K and V vectors and reuse them

text:
Paged KV Cache


Logical blocks: The model’s attention mechanism operates on the entire context as a single logical block (e.g., a 16K token context treated as one block for attention computations).
Physical blocks (pages): Memory is divided into smaller physical blocks/pages (e.g., 16–32 tokens each), dynamically allocated and mapped to different requests as needed.

Paged KV Cache - Multiple Requests


Each request’s KV cache is divided into multiple physical blocks (pages) that can be allocated independently.
Multiple requests can share the same physical blocks if they have similar context lengths, improving memory efficiency and GPU utilization.

Paged Attention


PagedAttention allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space

Computes attention across these non-contiguous blocks
This is done in a custom CUDA kernel optimized for the block-table lookup pattern

Inference vs Training
Training

Weight updates via backprop & gradient descent
Parallelizable across sequence length
Optimized for throughput

Inference

Optimized for latency (TTFT, ITL) and throughput simultaneously

\(\approx\) 1-1.5x model size at short context; can grow much larger when KV cache dominates

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Recap: Self-Attention




Project input vectors to query, key, and value spaces


\[\mathbf{queries} = X W_q\]
\[\mathbf{keys} = X W_k\]
\[\mathbf{values} = X W_v\]


Compute Similarity :


\[\mathbf{scores} = \mathbf{queries} \times \mathbf{keys}^T\]
\[\mathbf{attn\_weights} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{scores})\]


Contextualization


\[\mathbf{context\_vec} = \mathbf{attn\_weights} \times \mathbf{values}\]


\[
\mathbf{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathbf{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]







NOTE : Q is a function of the CURRENT token only. K and V are functions of ALL previous tokens

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Recap: Multi-Head Attention


Multi-Head Attention Overview

\(\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\)
\[\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)W^O\]
Scaled Dot-Product Attention:

\(Q, K, V\): Query, Key, and Value matrices derived from input embeddings
\(d_k\): The dimensionality of the keys (and queries)
\(W^O\): Output projection matrix that combines the outputs of all heads into a single vector.
\(h\): The number of parallel attention heads.

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
MHA - Generation Phase
Generation Phase (Autoregressive Decoding):

Generate tokens one at a time autoregressively
At each step, compute attention over all previously generated tokens
Keys and Values for past tokens remain unchanged
Only the new token’s Query needs to attend to all previous Keys/Values

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
MHA - Generation Phase


Problem: Without caching, we recompute K and V for all previous tokens at every step!

Step 1: Compute K, V for token 1
Step 2: Recompute K, V for tokens 1, 2
Step 3: Recompute K, V for tokens 1, 2, 3
…
Step N: Recompute K, V for all N tokens → O(N²) redundant computation


Solution: KV Cache - Store computed K and V vectors and reuse them

Note


The cache grows linearly with sequence length: long context is expensive in memory even though each new token is cheap in compute. This single fact motivates every attention variant that follows.

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)






Key Insight: Compress K and V into a low-dimensional latent vector before caching



Project hidden states into a compressed latent \(c^{KV}\) (512 dims)
Cache the latent plus a small decoupled RoPE key
Prefill / training (compute-bound, many queries) : materialise K, V from the latent - the up-projection amortises over the whole sequence
Decode (memory-bound, one query) : fold \(W^{K}\) into the query path and \(W^{V}\) into \(W^O\) - attend directly in latent space, never materialise K/V

section: Which Cost Center Does It Attack?
text:
Which Cost Center Does It Attack?
Every variant so far shrinks something. The useful question is which bill it reduces - and that follows from the two regimes.


Training & Prefill

Parallel over the sequence
Compute-bound (high AI)
What hurts: the \(O(S^2)\) term


Decode

Serial, one token at a time
Bandwidth-bound (AI < 1)
What hurts: bytes read per token









Important


Shrink the cache \(\rightarrow\) helps decode only. Training never reads a KV cache - it recomputes in parallel.
Shrink the interaction pattern \(\rightarrow\) attacks \(S^2\), which appears in training, prefill and decode.





Two sentences that partition the entire taxonomy.

MQA/GQA change nothing at training : with \(N\) query heads you compute \(N\) heads’ worth of scores no matter how many KV heads feed them
MLA is not fewer FLOPs at decode : it attends in the 512-dim latent for all heads. It trades FLOPs for bandwidth - deliberately moving right on the roofline, into headroom that was idle anyway
Linear attention’s pitch migrated : 2020 sold \(O(S)\) training; 2025 sells constant-state decode










Tip


Training is capex the lab pays once. Inference is opex that scales with every user, forever. That asymmetry is why architecture changes have drifted toward decode - and why inference is 80-90% of compute spend.



Everything so far made each remembered token cheaper. At 1M context that is no longer enough \(\rightarrow\) stop remembering most of them.

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
The Key Question

Is GPU spending its time doing compute or waiting for data?


To answer this, we need to understand:

Arithmetic Intensity - how much compute per byte of memory accessed
The Roofline Model - what limits the GPU’s performance
How prefill and decode differ - why decode is memory bound

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Arithmetic Intensity
\[\text{Arithmetic Intensity} = \frac{\text{Compute FLOPs}}{\text{Memory Bytes}}\]
AI tells you whether the model is spending time computing (doing math) or fetching (moving data).

Low AI = GPU mostly waiting for data.
High AI = GPU mostly doing useful computation.







Tip


Intuition : “Imagine you’re a cook. The fridge (HBM) is in the next room. Arithmetic intensity is how many dishes you can prepare per trip to the fridge.

If AI=1, you grab one ingredient, cook one dish, walk back. Terrible.
If AI=100, you grab one ingredient and cook 100 dishes. Great!”

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Arithmetic Intensity
Setup: Matrix multiply in a linear layer : \(Y = X \cdot W\)
B : batch size, D : hidden dimension, F : feedforward dimension


\(X\): B \(\times\) D, \(W\): D \(\times\) F
FLOPs = \(2 \cdot B \cdot D \cdot F\)
Bytes transferred:

Read X: \(B \cdot D \cdot 2\)
Read W: \(D \cdot F \cdot 2\)
Write Y: \(B \cdot F \cdot 2\)

Total Bytes = \(2(BD + DF + BF)\)

\[\text{AI} = \frac{2 \cdot B \cdot D \cdot F}{2(BD + DF + BF)}\]
\[= \frac{B \cdot D \cdot F}{BD + DF + BF}\]
If \(B \ll D, F\):
\[\text{AI} \approx \frac{B \cdot D \cdot F}{D \cdot F} = B\]


Arithmetic intensity \(\approx\) batch size (when B is small relative to model dimensions)

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Arithmetic Intensity
Batch Size = 1 (single-stream decode)
\[    \text{AI} = \frac{2 \cdot D \cdot F}{2 \cdot D \cdot F + 2 \cdot D + 2 \cdot F} \approx 1 \text{ FLOP/byte}\]



You read the entire weight matrix (\(D \times F\))…

…but only do one row’s worth of compute



For A100 GPU (Capacity : 150-200 FLOPs/byte):

AI \(\approx\) 1 \(\ll\) 150-200
Peak-compute upper bound: < 1% of peak FLOPs
The GPU is basically spending all its time waiting for data to arrive from memory, not doing math.

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
The Roofline Model


Performance is bounded by:

Compute : how fast GPU does math (FLOPs/s)
Bandwidth : how fast data moves (GB/s)
Capacity : whether weights + KV cache fit at all (GB)








Note


Knee point = bandwidth-bound to compute-bound transisiton -> minimum AI needed to fully utilize GPU’s compute.







Figure: an example roofline plot showing two algorithms with different arithmetic intensities (Algo 1 and Algo 2) and their corresponding theoretical peak throughput under different bandwidths (BW1 and BW2). In the red area, an algorithm is bandwidth bound at both bandwidths and is wasting some fraction of the hardware’s peak FLOPs/s. The yellow area is bandwidth-bound only at the lower bandwidth (BW1). The green area is compute-bound at all bandwidths.


\[\text{Performance} = \min(\text{Peak FLOPs}, \text{AI} \times \text{BW})\]

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Prefill vs Decode


Prefill

Process all prompt tokens at once
T = S (hundreds/thousands)
Parallelizable
Compute-bound (high AI)
Fills the KV cache
Determines TTFT


Decode

Generate tokens one at a time
T = 1
Sequential (autoregressive)
Memory-bound (low AI)
Reads from & appends to KV cache
Determines per-token latency (ITL)

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
MLP AI: Prefill vs Decode


Prefill (T = S)
\[\text{AI}_{\text{MLP}} \approx B \cdot S\]
Compute-bound

S = 1024, B = 1 : AI ≈ 1024
Well above knee point (~200)


Decode (T = 1)
\[\text{AI}_{\text{MLP}} \approx B\]
Memory-bound (BAD)

B = 1 => AI ≈ 1, B = 32 => AI ≈ 32
Far below knee point









Important


During decode, ALL model weights are read from HBM for every single output token, but only do one token’s worth of matmuls. GPU utilization: 1-5% of peak FLOPs.

Inference Metrics
User-facing:

TTFT : Time to First Token - How long user waits for the first word to appear. Dominated by prefill time.
ITL : Inter-Token Latency (Streaming speed) - how fast words appear after the first one (seconds/token).

System-facing: - - Throughput : Total tokens the system can produce per second across all users (tokens/sec).

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Key Inference Optimizations
Most optimizations map to one of four strategies:

Read less data per token

Quantization (smaller weights), GQA/MLA (smaller KV cache), pruning

Do more useful work per data read

Batching (amortize weight reads), kernel fusion (fewer HBM round trips)

Generate more tokens per forward pass

Speculative decoding (verify N tokens in one pass instead of generating 1)

Schedule / place work better

Continuous batching, prefix caching, prefill/decode disaggregation

title: LLM Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
The One Formula to Remember
\[\text{Decode tokens/sec} \approx \frac{\text{Memory Bandwidth (GB/s)}}{\text{Model Size (GB)} + \text{KV Cache Overhead (GB)}}\]

Three numbers determine decode performance:

Model size in bytes (reduce with quantization)
KV cache size (reduce with GQA, MLA, sliding window)
Memory bandwidth of GPU (more the better)
